nameStory: The name 'Donkey Tail' comes from the plant's thick, fleshy stems that trail and curve like a donkey's tail swishing back and forth. This Mediterranean native is also called 'myrtle spurge' because its blue-green leaves resemble those of myrtle shrubs, though the two plants aren't related.
description: Donkey Tail is a low-growing succulent with thick, rubbery stems that sprawl along the ground or cascade over rocks and walls. The plant forms dense mats up to 2 feet wide but rarely grows taller than 6-8 inches. Its distinctive blue-green, oval leaves spiral around the stems like tiny scales, giving it an almost reptilian appearance. In spring, bright yellow-green flower clusters appear at the stem tips.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, fleshy blue-green leaves shaped like teardrops, arranged in spirals around the stem. They feel rubbery and waxy to the touch, often with a powdery coating that rubs off on your fingers.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats with thick stems that trail along the ground or drape over walls. The whole plant has a succulent, almost artificial appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright chartreuse-yellow flower clusters appear at stem tips in late spring. The tiny flowers lack petals but are surrounded by showy, petal-like bracts.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, fleshy stems that feel firm and contain a milky white sap. When broken, they release this sticky latex that can irritate skin.

habitat: Found in sunny, well-drained locations like rock gardens, stone walls, and sandy slopes throughout New England. This escaped garden plant thrives in poor, rocky soils and is often seen in coastal areas where salt tolerance gives it an advantage. It particularly favors south-facing slopes and areas with excellent drainage.

seasonality.spring: Bright yellow-green flower clusters bloom from April through June, making this the easiest time for identification. New growth appears as the weather warms.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade but the distinctive blue-green spiral leaves remain prominent. Plants may produce small three-parted seed capsules.
seasonality.fall: Foliage persists through fall, though it may take on slightly more purple tints in cooler weather.
seasonality.winter: Evergreen leaves remain visible even under light snow cover, making winter identification possible in milder areas.

funFact: Despite being called 'myrtle spurge,' this plant is actually more closely related to poinsettias than to true myrtles, and like its festive cousin, it produces that same milky white sap that was once used to remove warts and moles in folk medicine.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other succulent garden plants, but the spiral arrangement of blue-green leaves is unique among spurges. Remember: if it looks like a succulent houseplant growing wild with leaves arranged like a spiral staircase, it's likely Donkey Tail.
contextualKnowledge: This is an invasive species that's banned for sale in several states due to its aggressive spreading habit. The milky sap can cause severe skin and eye irritation, so never handle this plant without gloves, especially when it's flowering or damaged.
compareHints: Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage. While cypress spurge also spreads aggressively, it has needle-like leaves, and spotted spurge is a flat, annual weed with tiny oval leaves that lack the distinctive blue-green color and spiral arrangement.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
